extracted.intended_audience: television news reporters (survey respondents) and media researchers
extracted.subtask_short: survey instrument for TV reporter influences
extracted.subtask_description: A questionnaire appendix from a dissertation measuring how often various external and internal actors (politicians, PR practitioners, advertisers/economic actors, managers) influence television news coverage, plus respondent/station demographics. Intended both as a data-collection instrument and a measurement specification for media-influence constructs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politicians/Government influence — which stories covered
rubrics_metrics.description: In your opinion, how often do politicians or government officials try to influence which stories are covered or emphasized? (Note: Sources of influence may include people/offices working for the politicians/officials.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Politicians/Government influence — how story is covered
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do politicians or government officials try to influence how a story is covered (e.g., the angle of a story or stance on an issue)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Politicians/Government influence — discourage coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do politicians or government officials try to influence journalists/stations not to cover (avoid covering) a particular story or topic?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of public relations materials as basis for stories
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do stations use public relations materials (e.g., broadcast news releases, video news releases) as the basis for a news story, including just sparking a story idea?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: PR influence — coverage/emphasis because of PR
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do journalists/stations cover or emphasize particular stories because of influences from public relations practitioners?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: PR influence — how a story is covered because of PR
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do journalists/stations cover a story in a certain way because of influences from public relations practitioners (e.g., the angle of a story or stance on an issue)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: PR influence — avoid covering because of PR
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do journalists/stations not cover (avoid covering) stories or topics because of influences from public relations practitioners?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency stations receive VNRs
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do stations receive video news releases (VNRs)? (Note: This does not include those received from or produced by government agencies.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7). Note excludes government-produced/received VNRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency stations use VNRs
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do stations use VNRs (can include just sparking an idea for a story)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency stations air VNRs with little/no editing
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do stations air VNRs with little to no editing?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived PR professionals' attempts — which stories covered
rubrics_metrics.description: In your opinion, how often do public relations professionals try to influence which stories are covered or emphasized?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived PR professionals' attempts — how story is covered
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do public relations professionals try to influence how a story is covered (e.g., the angle of a story or stance on an issue)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived PR professionals' attempts — discourage coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do public relations professionals try to influence journalists/stations not to cover (avoid covering) a particular story or topic?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived economic compromise of TV news content
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do you believe that television news content is compromised because of economic pressures?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic pressure — avoid stories damaging to organization's interests
rubrics_metrics.description: In your opinion, how often are journalists pressured to avoid covering certain stories (not cover them) because they might be damaging to the economic interests of the organization?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic pressure — special handling when company has economic clout
rubrics_metrics.description: How often are journalists pressured to specially handle stories involving companies or organizations with some economic clout over their station?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct superior suggestion — suggest to cover unusual stories
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do managers/superiors within TV stations (e.g., assignment editors, producers, news directors) directly suggest to reporters to cover a story that would normally not be covered? (Note: These suggestions include a superior directly instructing a reporter to take the action or providing overt instructions about what kinds of stories to cover/avoid and perhaps how to cover them.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7). Note clarifies examples of direct suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome — cover story because of direct suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do journalists cover the topic/story as a result of this type of suggestion?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct superior suggestion — suggest how to cover story
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do managers/superiors working within TV stations directly suggest how a story or topic should be covered (e.g., the angle of the story or stance on the issue)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome — cover story in way manager directly suggested
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do journalists cover the topic/story in the way the manager/superior directly suggested?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct superior instruction — tell journalists to avoid stories
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do managers/superiors directly tell journalists to avoid (not cover) certain stories, topics or issues?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome — purposely avoid because manager specifically told them
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do journalists purposely avoid (not cover) certain stories/topics because a manager/superior specifically tells them to take this action?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipatory self-censorship — avoid because of expected manager response
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do journalists purposely avoid (not cover) newsworthy stories because of how they believe their managers/superiors would respond?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipatory selection — choose/ emphasize because of expected manager response
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do journalists choose to cover or emphasize certain stories because of how they believe their managers/superiors would respond?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipatory framing — take particular angle because of expected manager response
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do journalists take a particular angle on a story because of how they believe their managers/superiors would respond?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect signals — suggest to cover stories via modeling/attention
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do managers/superiors within TV stations give indirect signals/suggestions to reporters to cover a story that normally would not be covered? (Note: Indirect signals might include purposely showing a reporter a similar type of story from another station, mentioning the topic/angle in passing, showing great interest in or airing this type of story, or positive reinforcement)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7). Note gives examples of indirect signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome — cover because of indirect suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do journalists cover the topic/story as a result of this type of suggestion?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect signals — indirectly signal how to cover (angle/stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do managers/superiors working within TV stations indirectly signal/suggest how a story or topic should be covered (e.g., the angle of the story or stance on the issue)? (Note: Indirect signals here may include mentioning the angle in passing conversation, showing how a similar type of story was covered from another station, showing great interest in a particular side of the story.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7). Note provides examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome — cover in way indirectly signaled by manager
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do journalists cover the topic/story in the way the manager/superior indirectly signaled/suggested?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect negative signals — subtle cues to avoid coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do journalists get indirect signals/suggestions (e.g., yawns/hemming/hawing, lack of interest in stories/don’t get aired, jokes) from their managers/superiors to avoid covering certain stories or topics?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7). Examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome — avoid coverage because of indirect negative signals
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do journalists purposely avoid (not cover) certain stories or topics because of these indirect signals/suggestions from managers/superiors?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: Almost Never — Very Often (1 to 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Years working in the television industry
rubrics_metrics.description: How many years have you worked in the television industry? _______ years
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open numeric response (years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Years working at current station
rubrics_metrics.description: How many years have you worked at your current station? _______ years
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open numeric response (years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership of station (type/category)
rubrics_metrics.description: To the best of your knowledge, the ownership of your station is: ○ family/independent ○ group—up to 4 stations total ○ group—5 to 10 stations total ○ group—more than 10 stations
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorical multiple-choice responses as listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-ownership of other media
rubrics_metrics.description: To the best of your knowledge, do the owners of your station also own other types of media (e.g., newspapers)? ○ No ○ Yes, up to 4 newspapers (or other type of media) ○ Yes, 5 to 10 newspapers (or other type of media) ○ Yes, more than 10 newspapers (or other type of media) ○ Don’t know
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorical multiple-choice responses including 'Don’t know'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Company ownership status (private/public/don't know)
rubrics_metrics.description: The company that owns your station is ○ privately owned ○ publicly owned—has publicly traded stock ○ don’t know
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-choice categorical response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size of news department (staff count category)
rubrics_metrics.description: What category best describes the number of people who work in your station’s news department? ○ 1-10 ○ 11-20 ○ 21-30 ○ 31-50 ○ 51+
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorical multiple-choice by staff-size ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent gender
rubrics_metrics.description: Your gender is ○ Male ○ Female ○ Decline to Answer
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-choice categorical response with explicit decline option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent age range
rubrics_metrics.description: What is your age? ○ 18-24 years ○ 25-34 years ○ 35-44 years ○ 45-54 years ○ 55-64 years ○ 65 years and over
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorical multiple-choice by age ranges.
